terms.comment: Morgan–Owens cites it from Holberg and Pallas (1811) onward. ignivomus, vomiting fire, is late Latin (Lactantius, Lewis & Short); Lucretius calls the crater of Etna its faucēs (6.630, Lewis & Short s.v. faucēs).
The god’s name made a common noun, as in the modern languages; Morgan–Owens cites it from Egger.

phrases.latin: Ecce, mōns fūmat! — Nōlī timēre: procul abest.
phrases.english: Look, the mountain’s smoking! — Don’t be afraid: it’s a long way off.

phrases.latin: Aetnaeī verticis fūmō ac murmure pavefactus
phrases.english: terrified by the smoke and rumbling of Etna’s summit

phrases.latin: interdumque ātram prōrumpit ad aethera nūbem turbine fūmantem piceō et candente favillā
phrases.english: and now it hurls up into the sky a black cloud, smoking with a pitchy whirl of smoke and glowing ash
